newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran moderate Khatami holds lead for presidency.
newsitem.headline: Iran moderate Khatami holds lead for presidency.

text.p: Moderate former culture minister Mohammad Khatami looked headed on Saturday for an upset victory in Iran's presidential election.

The Iranian news agency IRNA said latest "unofficial" figures showed Khatami, a moderate compared with most of the conservative Shi'ite Moslem clergymen who run the Islamic republic, had won 10,389,372 of the 15,367,108 votes counted so far.
His main rival, conservative parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri who had until recently been expected to become Iran's next president, won only 4,118,869 votes.
Two minor candidates won fewer than 400,000 votes apiece.
Analysts said if the trend continued, the result would be the biggest political upset in the history of Iran's 18-year-old revolution.

With 33 million people aged 15 and over eligible to vote, it remained to be seen if Khatami would head for a landslide or see his lead eroded by rural support for Nateq-Nouri. A candidate has to win half of all votes to win in the first round.

Nateq-Nouri is a traditionalist backed by influential conservative clerics and merchants. He was considered the establishment candidate and was expected to be stronger in rural areas, where vote counting was likely to take longer.

Alireza Tabesh, the official in charge of the election, said the turnout in Friday's ballot was "unprecedentedly heavy". Polling was extended for four additional hours because of queues of people waiting to vote.
The election was to choose a successor to President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, who must step down in August after serving the maximum two four-year terms allowed by law.

Campaigning was the fiercest political battle between conservative clerics and moderates since the 1979 Islamic revolution toppled the pro-American shah. Both Khatami and Nateq-Nouri are 54-year-old middle-ranking clergymen.
Khatami's campaign was backed by centrists close to Rafsanjani and Islamist left-wingers who have moderated many of their views in recent years.
The unlikely coalition was formed to counter conservatives which Khatami's backers accused of trying to monopolise state power by adding the presidency to their control of parliament.

Khatami owes his appeal to a reputation as an open-minded religious intellectual and tolerant politician. He gained wide support among women, young people and intellectuals who fear a harder application of Islamic rules in everyday life and restrictions on freedom of expression.

Khatami has advocated more personal freedom, domocracy and the rule of law in a country where many complain that state bodies act arbitrarily and rules change according to officials' personal preferences.
Khatami appears to have also drawn many votes from devout Iranians because he holds the title of Seyyed as someone believed to be a descendant of Islam's founder Prophet Mohammad.

All four candidates were screened by a conservative group of senior clergy and lawyers before being allowed to run. The group rejected 234 other candidates for failing to match up to Islamic revolutionary ideals.

Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who outranks the president, tacitly supported Nateq-Nouri. He said voters should choose someone who could "stand against America and those who want to impose their will on our nation".
